name: Moving Goalposts Pattern
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Target That Keeps Sliding Forward
lesson.summary: A recurring rhetorical pattern where a missed prediction is quietly replaced with a new, narrower or more distant milestone rather than acknowledged as a failure, building on the 3-5 Years Away Pattern and feeding directly into the Catalog of Broken Promises.
lesson.body:
Imagine someone tells you a bridge will be finished in three years. Three years pass, and the bridge is not finished. If they say "we underestimated, it will take five more years, and here is exactly why," that is an update. If instead they say "well, what we really meant by finished was that the foundation would be poured," while quietly setting a new three year clock for something they now call the real finish line, that is a moving goalpost. The distinguishing feature is not that the timeline changed. Timelines change all the time for good reasons. The distinguishing feature is that the definition of success changed at the exact moment the old definition was about to be violated.

Quantum computing commentary has a long running version of this pattern, and it connects directly to the 3-5 Years Away Pattern covered earlier. A specific capability gets promised on a specific horizon: quantum computers that break RSA encryption, quantum computers that design new drugs faster than any existing method, quantum computers that solve logistics problems no classical computer could touch. The horizon arrives. The capability has not. Rather than the community concluding that the original prediction was wrong, the goal quietly narrows. Breaking encryption becomes showing quantum advantage on a problem related to cryptography. Designing new drugs becomes simulating a small molecule that classical chemists could already simulate, just somewhat differently. Each narrowed goal gets its own fresh three to five year horizon, and the cycle restarts.

This is worth taking seriously as a pattern rather than dismissing as simple dishonesty, because it usually is not driven by bad faith. Research genuinely is hard to predict, and a scientist who narrows scope after discovering a problem is much harder than expected is doing something reasonable. The trouble is structural: there is rarely a public accounting of the fact that the goal changed. The old promise simply stops being mentioned, the new one is presented as though it had always been the real target, and an observer not tracking history closely has no way to notice anything shifted.

The practical damage this does is that it makes the field's overall track record impossible to evaluate honestly. Every entry in a Catalog of Broken Promises could, in principle, be defended by its author as "that is not really what I meant" after the fact, and if the goalposts are allowed to move freely, no claim can ever be definitively marked as failed. A field where every prediction is retroactively adjustable can claim an unbroken record of success no matter what actually happens, which is precisely why tracking claims by their original wording and deadline, before any post hoc softening, matters so much.

A useful defense against this pattern is to write predictions down, with dates and concrete criteria, before the deadline arrives, and then hold the later conversation to that original text rather than to whatever the speaker now says they meant. If a specific person or organization promised fault tolerant, error corrected quantum computers with a million physical qubits by a specific year, and that year passes with a few hundred qubits and no error correction at scale, the honest response is that the prediction was wrong, not a quiet substitution of a smaller claim wearing the old prediction's clothes. Recognizing this pattern also sets up the next two chapters, on timelines built so vaguely they can never be falsified, and on the related trick of redefining what counts as success after the fact.
